notes.meaning: Jeremiah sent a letter from Jerusalem to the surviving leaders, priests, prophets, and ordinary people who had been taken to Babylon. Even though they were far away from the temple, God still reached out to instruct and comfort them. A written letter from a true prophet carried the same divine authority as a sermon spoken in person.

This letter was written after King Jeconiah, his mother Queen Nehushta, and the royal court had been taken away in 597 BC. The Babylonians also carried off skilled workers like craftsmen and metalsmiths to prevent weapons from being made. Stripping Jerusalem of its leaders and builders left the city weak and dependent.

King Zedekiah sent two royal messengers, Elasah and Gemariah, on an official visit to King Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah trusted these envoys to carry his prophetic letter to the exiles alongside their official business. Both men came from respected families that had helped King Josiah reform the nation and had protected Jeremiah in the past.

The letter opens with the Lord reminding the people that He Himself sent them into exile. Even though Nebuchadnezzar's army conquered them, Babylon was only God's instrument to discipline His people. The Lord of hosts was still their sovereign ruler and had not abandoned His covenant with them.

God commands the exiles to build houses, plant gardens, and eat the food they grow. This told them they were going to stay in Babylon for a very long time, rather than going home quickly. They were treated leniently enough by Babylon to own homes and work the land in peace.

God tells the exiles to marry, have children, and help their sons and daughters find spouses. He intended for their community to multiply and stay strong rather than slowly fade away in a foreign land. Their time in Babylon would span multiple generations before the return took place.

God directs the exiles to seek the welfare and peace of the pagan city where they were sent, and to pray to the Lord for it. If Babylon enjoyed peace and stability, the captive Israelites would also live safely and quietly. Praying for the good of their enemies was a demanding command that showed genuine trust in God's care.

The exiles are warned not to let false prophets, fortunetellers, or dream interpreters mislead them. The people had been encouraging these false teachers by eagerly asking for pleasant dreams and promises of quick rescue. Believing smooth lies would only keep them from accepting God's true plan.

These deceitful men claimed to speak on behalf of the Lord, but the Lord never sent them or gave them a message. They spoke only their own imaginations and the hopes of the crowds. Following self-appointed messengers always leads away from God's truth.

The Lord makes it clear that the exile in Babylon would last seventy full years before He would step in. Only when that entire appointed period was finished would He fulfill His promise to bring them back home. Knowing this set time was meant to put an end to false hopes of an early return.

God assures His people that His thoughts toward them are purposeful and kind, aimed at their ultimate peace and well-being rather than their destruction. Even during their hard discipline in exile, God had not forgotten them. He was preparing a real future and an enduring hope for their nation.

differ.view: Many evangelicals teach that while this promise was originally given to Israel under judgment, all believers can trust God's good purposes through Christ, even though it does not promise a life free of earthly suffering.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: A popular modern teaching takes this verse out of its historical setting and claims it guarantees personal wealth, good health, and worldly success to individual believers today.

notes.meaning: When the time for rescue arrived, God would move His people to call out to Him in sincere prayer. Prayer was not a substitute for God's promise, but the very way His people would receive it. Whenever God prepares to show mercy, He first gives His people a heart to pray.

The Lord promises that those who search for Him with an undivided heart will truly find Him. The trials of exile were meant to turn them away from idols and lead them into genuine repentance. God always responds to wholehearted faith and honest devotion.

God declares that He will allow Himself to be found by His people and will end their long captivity. He will gather them back together not just from Babylon, but from every place to which they had been scattered. He who scattered them in judgment will surely bring them back home in mercy.

Some exiles boasted that God had raised up local prophets for them in Babylon, making Jeremiah's letters unnecessary. These self-proclaimed prophets were telling the people what they wanted to hear. Jeremiah directly confronts this foolish confidence.

God turns the discussion toward King Zedekiah and the citizens who were still living back in Jerusalem. The exiles thought those left behind were more fortunate, but God explains that their position was actually far worse. Having a king on David's throne would not shield Jerusalem from coming judgment.

God warns that war, famine, and sickness will strike the people remaining in Jerusalem. He compares them to rotten, spoiled figs that are so foul nobody can eat them. This reminded the exiles of Jeremiah's earlier vision showing that the worst calamity was reserved for those left in the city.

The Lord will chase the unrepentant survivors with disaster and scatter them among foreign kingdoms. Their ruin would be so total that surrounding nations would gasp in shock and use their name in curses. God's holiness demands that unfaithfulness brings severe consequences.

This harsh judgment came because the people constantly ignored God's words sent through the prophets time and again. God had patiently reached out to warn them, but both the citizens of Jerusalem and many exiles refused to listen. Despising God's messengers is the same as despising God Himself.

God calls upon every exile living in Babylon to stop and listen carefully to His word. Both the faithful believers and those who had gone astray needed to hear what God was about to do. God was about to expose the false leaders who had been misleading the community.

The Lord names two specific false prophets in Babylon, Ahab and Zedekiah, who were telling lies in His name. These men were encouraging rebellion against Babylon, leading King Nebuchadnezzar to arrest them. God announced that the Babylonian king would execute them publicly right before the eyes of the exiles.

Nebuchadnezzar executed Ahab and Zedekiah by roasting them alive in the fire, a typical Babylonian punishment for treason. Their agonizing death became so infamous that Jewish exiles turned it into a common curse against their worst enemies. When God exposes false prophets, their pride turns into enduring shame.

God reveals that these two men were guilty of terrible secret sins, including committing adultery with their neighbors' wives. They acted corruptly in secret while pretending to deliver holy messages from God. Even though they hid their crimes from the public, God saw everything and stood as an eyewitness against them.

Jeremiah was given another message, this time directed against Shemaiah, another false prophet in Babylon. Shemaiah was furious over Jeremiah's letter and tried to take matters into his own hands. God holds individuals accountable whenever they try to silence His truth.

Shemaiah had sent letters in his own name from Babylon back to Jerusalem, writing directly to the priests and to Zephaniah the leading temple officer. He acted completely on his own authority without any message or permission from God. He wanted the authorities in Jerusalem to stop Jeremiah's ministry by force.

In his letter, Shemaiah told Zephaniah that God had made him the temple overseer in place of the former priest Jehoiada. He claimed it was Zephaniah's duty to control any wild, raving person who claimed to be a prophet. Shemaiah demanded that Jeremiah be locked up in the stocks and neck irons like a madman.

Shemaiah boldly scolded the priest in Jerusalem for failing to arrest and punish Jeremiah of Anathoth. He accused Jeremiah of being a fake who merely acted like a prophet. False teachers often become angry and aggressive when their deceit is uncovered by God's truth.

Shemaiah's complaint was that Jeremiah had sent word to Babylon telling the captives that their exile would be long. Jeremiah had instructed them to build houses and plant gardens instead of packing to go home. This sound advice wrecked Shemaiah's false promises of an immediate return.

Instead of arresting Jeremiah, Zephaniah the priest read Shemaiah's angry letter aloud to him. This warned Jeremiah about the plots being made against him by the false prophets in Babylon. Zephaniah showed enough wisdom to hear what Jeremiah had to say rather than blindly obeying Shemaiah.

As soon as Jeremiah heard the letter read, the Lord gave him a direct answer. God never leaves His servants without guidance when they face threats from opponents. The Lord was ready to deliver a formal sentence against Shemaiah's rebellion.

God ordered Jeremiah to write back to the exiles in Babylon to expose Shemaiah's lies. The Lord had never called Shemaiah, yet he had caused the community to place their faith in empty falsehoods. Leading God's people into false hope is a serious offense that brings divine judgment.

The Lord sentenced Shemaiah by announcing that his family line would be cut off entirely, leaving him with no descendants among God's people. Shemaiah himself would never live to see the joyful restoration God had planned for Israel. Because he preached rebellion against the Lord's word, he lost every part in the blessing to come.
